text: s of the injected area.23 Thermal, laser, or multipolar (coaptive) or plasma electro- coagulative endoscopic techniques are also of benefit, and again there is no clear evidence to prefer one over anoth- er.22 Combining injection with thermal coagulation may be of greater benefit than either alone; UK guidelines con- sider it may be better in a subset of patients with active arterial bleeding, although it is not considered to offer ad- ditional benefit in most patients,23 while subsequent Cana- dian guidelines consider the combination superior.22 The use of mechanical clips may also be effective,22,23 espe- cially for actively bleeding large vessels.23 If endoscopic treatments fail to stop bleeding, or rebleeding occurs, fur- ther endoscopic therapy may be considered, but otherwise patients require surgery.22,23 There is good evidence from systematic review24 that treatment with PPIs reduces rebleeding and surgery in pa- tients with acute bleeding peptic ulcers; one such review did not show reduced mortality,24 although others consider it to have been demonstrated.22 An intravenous bolus of a PPI followed by continuous infusion is recommended in patients who have undergone successful endoscopic ther- apy.22,23 There is no evidence that any PPI is superior to others.22,25 Some suggest that high-dose PPI therapy (oral or intravenous, depending on the degree of risk) should also be considered in patients awaiting endoscopy.22 In contrast, there is no evidence that H2-antagonists are of benefit in the treatment of acute nonvariceal bleeding, and somatostatin, octreotide, or tranexamic acid are not recom- mended.22,23 Eradication of H. pylori is recommended in those patients positive for the organism;22,23 eradication therapy is supe- rior to antisecretory drugs alone in preventing rebleed- ing.26 1.
